Test zulake against a live ADLS Gen2 account

Source: vignettes/articles/live-azure.Rmd
live-azure.Rmd

This guide is for whoever runs zulake’s tests against a real Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 account. It describes the live test the package has now, how to run it, and the further live tests worth writing. None of the code on this page runs when the site is built, because it needs an Azure account and a token.

What a live account adds

zulake’s Azure backend is tested in three layers. A fake over the fixtures and the recorded cassettes run everywhere, CRAN included. Azurite, Microsoft’s emulator, runs in CI against deltalake 1.7.0 reading the same tables. The third layer, one table on ADLS Gen2, runs only when someone with an account runs it.

Azurite is an independent implementation of the Blob REST API, so it catches most mistakes. It does not show these, which only Azure does:

Behaviour Azurite Azure
A rejected token 403 401, and zulake then asks for a new token once
Access control any token its --oauth basic mode accepts Entra ID roles: “Storage Blob Data Reader” is needed, “Reader” is not enough
Hierarchical namespace none real directories, which a listing can return as entries
The dfs endpoint none abfss:// and https://<account>.dfs… URIs name it, and zulake sends their requests to the blob endpoint
Tokens an unsigned test JWT real tokens that expire after about an hour
Certificates a test CA passed to zuhttp the public certificate chain
Tables written by Spark or Databricks only what was uploaded the files and directories those writers leave

Set up an account

You need a storage account with the hierarchical namespace on, a container, and the “Storage Blob Data Reader” role on that container for whoever runs the tests. “Storage Blob Data Contributor” is needed only to upload tables. With the Azure CLI:

az storage account create --name <account> --resource-group <group> \
  --kind StorageV2 --hns true --sku Standard_LRS
az storage container create --account-name <account> --name lake --auth-mode login
az role assignment create --assignee <you-or-app-id> \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Reader" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<group>/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/<account>/blobServices/default/containers/lake"

Then upload a table. The example table the package ships is small and has partitions, a delete and in-commit timestamps:

az storage blob upload-batch --account-name <account> --auth-mode login \
  --destination lake/orders --source "$(Rscript -e 'cat(system.file("extdata", "orders", package = "zulake"))')"

Uploading sets each blob’s Last-Modified to the time of the upload. A table without in-commit timestamps takes its commit times from those, so its times on Azure are not the ones its local copy has. live.py asks deltalake about the uploaded table itself, so the comparison still holds.

Run the live suite

tests/testthat/test-azure-live.R opens one table and compares zulake with deltalake 1.7.0 reading the same table. It checks the version, the live files and every row. It also checks that the three URI forms give the same files, and that the token appears nowhere in the snapshot, its print or an auth error. Locally:

export ZULAKE_AZURE_URI=abfss://lake@<account>.dfs.core.windows.net/orders
export ZULAKE_AZURE_TOKEN="$(az account get-access-token \
  --resource https://storage.azure.com --query accessToken --output tsv)"
(cd tools/oracle && uv run --frozen python live.py /tmp/zulake-live)
R CMD INSTALL .
ZULAKE_AZURE_ANSWERS=/tmp/zulake-live Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "azure-live")'

In CI, .github/workflows/azure-live.yaml does the same on dispatch (gh workflow run azure-live.yaml --ref main). It logs in with a federated credential from the repository secrets AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID and AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, and reads the table named by ZULAKE_AZURE_URI. It fails if the suite skips. Its log goes on #24.

Live tests worth adding

Each test below states what it checks, its oracle, and what it needs on the account. They would go in test-azure-live.R and skip, like the existing one, when the variables are unset. A test that needs a second table or identity reads it from a variable of its own, such as ZULAKE_AZURE_URI_DV.

Every fixture table

Upload all 31 tables from tests/testthat/fixtures/tables/ under one prefix and loop the existing comparison over them, with live.py run once per table. This is the strongest single test. It covers deletion vectors, V2 and multi-part checkpoints, column mapping, log compaction, and the refusals of unsupported reader features, all over the network. The oracle is deltalake reading the same blobs. Refused tables (zl-unknown-reader-feature, column_mapping_id_mode) must still give the same error class as they do locally.

for (name in strsplit(Sys.getenv("ZULAKE_AZURE_TABLES"), ",")[[1]]) {
  uri <- paste0(Sys.getenv("ZULAKE_AZURE_ROOT"), "/", name)
  tbl <- lake_open(uri, credentials = credentials)
  expect_oracle(lake_version(tbl), name, lake_version(tbl), "loaded_version")
}

A table written by Databricks or Spark

Uploaded tables hold only the files the fixtures have. A table that a real writer created on ADLS also has directory entries in the hierarchical namespace, .crc files next to the commits and, from Databricks, deletion vectors and V2 checkpoints with sidecars. deltalake reading it is the oracle. Run lake_files() and lake_read() at the latest version and at one older version.

The token is asked for again after a 401

Azure answers a token it rejects with 401, and zulake then calls credentials() once more. Azurite answers 403, so this path has never run against a real service. Count the calls with a function whose first token is malformed:

calls <- 0
credentials <- function() {
  calls <<- calls + 1
  if (calls == 1) "not-a-token" else Sys.getenv("ZULAKE_AZURE_TOKEN")
}
tbl <- lake_open(Sys.getenv("ZULAKE_AZURE_URI"), credentials = credentials)
expect_identical(calls, 2)
expect_identical(nrow(lake_read(tbl)), as.integer(lake_count(tbl)))

A token that is still rejected the second time must give zulake_error_auth with status 401 and Azure’s code.

An identity without the data role

A service principal with “Reader” on the account but no data role is refused with 403 AuthorizationPermissionMismatch. zulake must raise zulake_error_auth with that code, before reading any data, and the error must not contain the token. This needs a second identity, whose token goes in ZULAKE_AZURE_TOKEN_NO_DATA.

Missing account, container and table

Each failure has its own answer from Azure, and each maps to a class:

URI Azure zulake
an account that does not exist DNS failure zulake_error_storage, with zuhttp’s reason
a container that does not exist 404 ContainerNotFound on the first listing zulake_error_not_table, as for an empty listing
a prefix with no _delta_log/ an empty listing zulake_error_not_table, and lake_is_table() is FALSE

The oracle is the class and its fields. The test also checks that none of these errors contains the token.

A public container

With anonymous read access on a second container, lake_open(uri, credentials = NULL) must read the table with no Authorization header and never retry. Azure accounts often disallow public access, so this test may have to wait for a dedicated account.

Names that need encoding

Upload a table under a prefix with a space, a %, a + and a non-ASCII letter (lake/a b%+ü/orders), and give each of the three URI forms percent-encoded and plain. Azure decodes paths differently from Azurite in corner cases. The oracle is deltalake on the same table, and the three URI forms must agree with it and with each other. zl-partitioned adds partition values that need encoding in file paths.

A log longer than one listing page

List Blobs returns at most 5,000 entries per page, so a _delta_log/ with more than that is read in pages. Write 5,100 commits with deltalake straight to the account, then compare lake_versions() and lake_version() with deltalake. The fake already pages, but only a real listing shows the markers Azure returns.

Time travel on a live table

Open the table, append a commit with deltalake, and check four things. The old snapshot still returns the old version and rows. lake_load() sees the new version. lake_load(timestamp =) with a time between the two commits returns the old version. lake_changes() from the old version to the new one lists the appended file.

Ranged reads and footers

lake_count(footers = TRUE) and the reading of deletion vectors use Range requests. On a table with large Parquet files (hundreds of megabytes), compare lake_count(footers = TRUE) with deltalake’s row count. The test also checks, by timing, that the footers are fetched without downloading whole files.

A token that expires during a long read

Real tokens last about an hour. Use lake_walk() on a table big enough to take longer than that, with a credentials function that fetches a new token from az each time it is called. The walk must finish, and the function must be called more than once. This test is slow, so it belongs in a dispatch of its own.
